questions.title: Ball Stops on the Clubhouse Patio
questions.question: Your ball lands on the patio behind the green, close to the clubhouse. The patio counts as something you cannot move (an immovable obstruction), and it is not out of bounds. What should you do?

choices.text: Hit the ball from where it is.
Move your ball for free and drop it nearby.
Drop your ball nearby, but add one penalty stroke.
The ball is out of bounds.

questions.explanation: Because the patio cannot be moved and it is not out of bounds, you can pick up your ball and drop it at the nearest place that gets you off the patio, with no extra shots added.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: Something on the course you cannot move, like a path, a wall, or the clubhouse patio.
A place where you are not allowed to play the ball, usually outside the golf course.
You can move your ball to a better spot without getting a penalty.

questions.teachingTip: When your ball ends up on something big and fixed, like a patio or a path, teach children that golf lets them move the ball to a safe place, for free.
likelyMisconceptions: Some children may think the patio is always out of bounds.
Some might try to play from the patio, which is risky and not needed.
Some may think they have to take a penalty to move the ball.

questions.title: Ball on the Clubhouse Patio (Immovable Obstruction)
questions.question: Your approach shot finishes on the clubhouse patio behind the green. The patio is in bounds and is treated as an immovable obstruction. What is the correct ruling?

choices.text: Play the ball as it lies.
The ball is out of bounds.

questions.explanation: As the patio is an immovable obstruction and is in bounds, the player is entitled to free relief under Rule 16.1. The ball is not out of bounds, nor is a penalty required.
